input.question: Why does a hearing a recording of my voice sound different to me then when I hear myself talk?
input.ground_truth: We hear sounds as vibrations hitting our ear drums. When we hear most sounds, these vibrations travel through the air and into the ear canal. Our own voices also vibrate through our bodies, creating a slightly lower pitch. When you hear a recording of your voice you are missing this extra level of vibration that lowers the sound, so your voice sounds higher than what you are used to. Source: _URL_0_

Question: Why does a hearing a recording of my voice sound different to me then when I hear myself talk?

Answer:

response.prediction: When you hear your voice in a recording, it sounds different from how you usually hear it because of the way sound travels. Normally, your voice reaches your ears in two ways: through the air (air conduction) and through the bones of your skull (bone conduction). The bones in your head transmit sound more efficiently, making your voice sound deeper and richer to yourself. However, when you listen to a recording, you only hear the sound as it travels through the air, which usually makes your voice sound higher and sometimes less pleasant to your own ears. That’s why your recorded voice can sound surprising or unfamiliar compared to what you hear while speaking.
